questions.q: Per this lesson, why is a properly bulkified Apex trigger a clear example of the performance-vs-complexity tradeoff?
options: Bulkification eliminates governor limits entirely, so there is no remaining tradeoff
Bulkified triggers always run slower than naive triggers, but are easier to maintain
It performs far better under load than a naive one-query-per-record trigger, but it's harder to read, harder to test fully, and easier to get subtly wrong
Salesforce no longer allows unbulkified triggers to be deployed at all
questions.explain: A bulkified trigger collects records into a set and issues one query for the batch instead of one per record -- a real performance win that comes with real added complexity and more ways to introduce a subtle bug.

questions.q: What is a 'selective query,' and what does achieving one require from the architect?
options: A query that returns a random sample of records; it requires no special design
A query that bypasses field-level security to run faster
A query that only runs in asynchronous Apex context
A query that filters on indexed fields so Salesforce can avoid a full table scan; achieving one requires understanding which fields are actually indexed and designing around that
questions.explain: Selective queries rely on indexed fields (standard indexes, External ID/Unique custom fields, or a requested custom index) in the WHERE clause -- getting this right means designing the query and often the data model around which fields are indexed, not just writing the query that reads most naturally.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the cost of a denormalized nightly reporting object that makes dashboards load instantly?
options: A batch job, a sync-timing lag, and an extra moving part that can silently drift out of date if the batch fails
There is no cost -- denormalization is strictly an improvement with no downside
It permanently disables the original source object
It requires disabling multi-factor authentication for reporting users
questions.explain: Denormalization trades read-time performance for a new maintenance burden: a batch job that has to run correctly, a lag between when source data changes and when the reporting object reflects it, and a new failure mode if the batch job breaks.

questions.q: What does this lesson mean by 'premature optimization,' and why does it call it a mistake?
options: Optimizing a system is always premature and should never be done
Adding performance-driven complexity before there's measured evidence of a real bottleneck -- it pays the full complexity cost for a performance gain nobody actually needed yet
Running a performance test before writing any code
Choosing Apex over Flow for a high-volume automation
questions.explain: The lesson recommends building the simple version first, measuring where it actually struggles under real load, and spending the complexity budget exactly there -- optimizing before that evidence exists spends the cost without a confirmed benefit.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why does it matter whether added complexity is 'isolated or spreads,' such as a caching layer behind one service class versus copy-pasted caching logic across a dozen Apex classes?
options: It doesn't matter -- all complexity costs the same regardless of where it lives
Spread-out complexity is always cheaper because it avoids a single point of failure
Isolated complexity is a manageable, contained cost, while complexity that spreads across many places compounds the maintenance burden every time any one of those places is touched
Salesforce automatically consolidates duplicated logic across Apex classes, so this concern doesn't apply
questions.explain: A single well-tested service class containing caching logic is one place to get right and maintain. The same logic duplicated with slightly different invalidation rules across a dozen classes turns one complexity cost into many, each one a separate risk of drift or bugs.
